s.u1.title: When forces cancel, and when they do not
s.u1.blurb: Two forces on one thing. Either they come to nothing, or what is left over makes it move.
s.u2.title: The first law
s.u2.blurb: What a thing does when nothing is acting on it, which is the question nobody thought to ask for two thousand years.
s.u3.title: Inertia has a number
s.u3.blurb: Everything resists being started and resists being stopped. How much is its mass.
s.u4.title: Momentum
s.u4.blurb: Mass on its own is not dangerous and speed on its own is not dangerous. The product of the two is.
s.u5.title: The second law
s.u5.blurb: Force equals mass times acceleration, and where that comes from.
s.u6.title: The third law
s.u6.blurb: Every push comes with a push back. The two never cancel, because they are never on the same thing.
ch8.u1.force:
Nobody has ever seen a force. You only ever see what one did.

A push on a trolley, a pull on a drawer, a hockey stick striking a ball: all three are forces, and you know they happened because something changed. A force can make a thing move, make a moving thing go faster or slower, turn it in a new direction, or squash it into a different shape. A spring stretched between two hands and a rubber ball pressed flat are both forces made visible.

So the question for this chapter is not what a force is. It is what a force does, and exactly how much.
a.ch8-u1-read-1.title: What a force actually does
ch8.u1.lab.predict.prompt: The floor pushes back on this box with 4 newtons of friction. You push it with 2 newtons. What happens over the next six seconds?
ch8.u1.lab.observe: Run the first task and watch both the box and the graphs.
ch8.u1.lab.explain:
Two newtons of push against four newtons of friction leaves nothing over. The forces are balanced, so the box stays exactly where it is, and both graphs stay flat.

Friction is not a fixed four newtons that always acts. It is the floor refusing to let go, and it refuses only as hard as it has to, up to its limit. Push harder than that limit and there is something left over, which is the unbalanced force that finally moves the box.
ch8.u1.lab.t1.label: Push with 2 newtons.
ch8.u1.lab.t1.asks: Nothing moved. How much force is the floor supplying, and how do you know?
ch8.u1.lab.t2.label: Push with exactly 4 newtons.
ch8.u1.lab.t2.asks: Still nothing. The two forces are now equal in size and opposite in direction. What is that called?
ch8.u1.lab.t3.label: Push with 10 newtons.
ch8.u1.lab.t3.asks: Now it goes. Six newtons are left over after the friction. Which graph shows you that most clearly?
ch8.u1.lab.closing: A balanced pair of forces changes nothing. Only what is left over after they have cancelled, the unbalanced force, moves anything.
a.ch8-u1-lab-2.title: Push it and nothing happens
a.ch8-u1-lab-2.blurb: A heavy box on a rough floor. The friction is set to 4 newtons, and you choose the push.
ch8.u1.draw.caption: A box being pushed across a rough floor, with the two forces acting along it marked.
ch8.u1.draw.box.label: The box, and the floor
ch8.u1.draw.box.do: Rule a line across the page for the floor, and draw a rectangle sitting on it. That rectangle is the only object in this picture, and every force you draw has to be acting on it.
ch8.u1.draw.box.does: Choosing one object first is the habit worth building. Half of all force mistakes come from drawing an arrow for a force that is acting on something else.
ch8.u1.draw.push.label: The push
ch8.u1.draw.push.do: Draw an arrow inside the box pointing the way you are pushing. Make its length mean something: a longer arrow is a bigger force.
ch8.u1.draw.push.does: This is the force you are supplying. It is the only one in the picture that somebody chose.
ch8.u1.draw.friction.label: The friction
ch8.u1.draw.friction.do: Draw a second arrow inside the box pointing the opposite way, and make it exactly as long as the first. Nothing moves yet.
ch8.u1.draw.friction.does: Friction comes from the floor and the bottom of the box rubbing together. It always points against the way the box is going or trying to go, and it never starts anything moving.
ch8.u1.draw.friction.p0: Friction is not a fixed number sitting there waiting. The floor pushes back only as hard as it has to.
ch8.u1.draw.friction.p1: Push with 2 N and the floor supplies 2 N. Push with 3 N and it supplies 3 N. The box still does not move.
ch8.u1.draw.friction.p2: There is a limit to what it can supply. Past that limit something is left over, and the box starts to move.
ch8.u1.draw.friction.p3: Which is why a heavy almirah needs a hard shove to start and much less to keep going.
ch8.u1.draw.net.label: What is left over
ch8.u1.draw.net.do: Now push harder. Above the box, draw your new push as one long arrow starting from the same place, and put a short cross-stroke on it at the point where the friction arrow would have reached. Everything past that stroke is the unbalanced force.
ch8.u1.draw.net.does: The part before the stroke has been cancelled by the friction and does nothing at all. Only the part beyond it moves the box. Shorten your push until the stroke sits at the tip, and the box stops moving however hard both forces are working.
ask.ch8-u1-draw-3.nomove.q: If the box is already sliding at a steady speed, what do the arrows look like?
ask.ch8-u1-draw-3.nomove.a:
Exactly equal again, and pointing opposite ways.

This is the part that catches people. A box that is moving steadily has no unbalanced force on it at all. You are still pushing, and the friction is still there, and the two have come into balance.

So a steady speed and standing still are the same situation as far as the forces go. In both, nothing is left over. The difference between them is only what the box happened to be doing when the forces balanced.
a.ch8-u1-draw-3.title: Draw the forces on a box
a.ch8-u1-draw-3.blurb: Four steps, and at the end you can look at a picture and say whether the box moves.
ch8.u1.sort.i0.label: A book lying on a table
ch8.u1.sort.i0.why: Nothing about it is changing, so whatever is acting on it has already cancelled.
ch8.u1.sort.i1.label: A cyclist speeding up on a flat road
ch8.u1.sort.i1.why: The velocity is changing, and only something left over can change it.
ch8.u1.sort.i2.label: A car braking hard
ch8.u1.sort.i2.why: Slowing is a change of velocity just as much as speeding up is.
ch8.u1.sort.i3.label: A lorry rolling along a level road at a steady 40 km/h
ch8.u1.sort.i3.why: Steady velocity means nothing is left over. The engine's push and the resistance have come into balance.
ch8.u1.sort.i4.label: Two children pulling a rope in opposite directions, neither moving
ch8.u1.sort.i4.why: Equal and opposite on the same rope, so the rope stays put.
ch8.u1.sort.i5.label: A ball swinging round on the end of a string at a steady speed
ch8.u1.sort.i5.why: The direction of the velocity is changing every instant, and that takes a force. Steady speed is not the test.
a.ch8-u1-sort-4.title: Balanced or unbalanced?
ch8.u1.quiz.q0.prompt: What does an unbalanced force do to an object?
ch8.u1.quiz.q0.o0: It changes its speed, its direction, or both
ch8.u1.quiz.q0.f0: Right. A change of velocity is the one thing only an unbalanced force can produce.
ch8.u1.quiz.q0.o1: It keeps it moving at a steady speed
ch8.u1.quiz.q0.f1: A steady speed needs no unbalanced force. It needs the forces to have cancelled.
ch8.u1.quiz.q0.o2: It holds it exactly where it is
ch8.u1.quiz.q0.f2: Holding something still is what balanced forces do.
ch8.u1.quiz.q1.prompt: You push a crate across a floor at a perfectly steady speed. What are the forces on it doing?
ch8.u1.quiz.q1.f0: Right. Steady velocity means nothing is left over, even though two forces are hard at work.
ch8.u1.quiz.q1.f1: If the push were winning it would be speeding up, not holding a steady speed.
ch8.u1.quiz.q1.f2: There is plenty of friction. It is exactly cancelling your push.
ch8.u1.quiz.q2.prompt: Friction acts on a box you are pushing. Which way does it point?
ch8.u1.quiz.q2.o0: Opposite to the way the box moves or tries to move
ch8.u1.quiz.q2.f0: Right. Friction only ever opposes, which is why it can never start anything moving.
ch8.u1.quiz.q2.o1: The same way as the push, helping it along
ch8.u1.quiz.q2.f1: Friction never drives anything. It only resists.
ch8.u1.quiz.q2.f2: That is the weight of the box, a different force entirely.
a.ch8-u1-quiz-5.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
ch8.u2.galileo:
For two thousand years everyone agreed that rest was the natural state of things. Push a ball and it rolls; stop pushing and it stops. The conclusion looks obvious: motion needs a cause, and when the cause goes the motion goes.

Galileo asked a different question. He let a marble roll down one slope and up another, and noticed that it climbed back to almost the height it started from. Make the second slope gentler and it still reached that height, travelling further to do it. So what happens if the second slope is made flat?

It would never reach the height. It would keep going, looking for it, forever.

Real marbles stop, of course, because of friction. Galileo's point was that friction is the reason, not the nature of motion. Newton turned that into the first law: an object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed, unless an unbalanced force makes it do otherwise.

No force is needed to keep something moving. A force is needed only to change how it is moving.
a.ch8-u2-read-1.title: Galileo rolls a marble downhill
ch8.u2.carom.predict.prompt: You strike the bottom coin of a neat pile with a fast striker. What happens to the coins above it?
ch8.u2.carom.predict.o0: The whole pile is knocked across the board
ch8.u2.carom.predict.o1: The pile drops straight down, almost where it was
ch8.u2.carom.predict.o3: The coins fly off in all directions
ch8.u2.carom.observe: Do it several times and watch the top of the pile, not the coin you hit.
ch8.u2.carom.explain:
The striker touches only the bottom coin, so only the bottom coin is given a force. The rest were at rest and had nothing acting on them sideways, so they stayed where they were and simply dropped as their support disappeared.

A slow push would have dragged the whole pile along, because friction between the coins would have had time to carry the force upwards. The hit has to be fast for exactly that reason.
ch8.u2.do.steps:
1. Stack six or seven coins in a neat pile on a smooth table.
2. Put one more coin flat on the table, a little way off, and line it up with the bottom coin of the pile.
3. Flick it hard and low, so it strikes only the bottom coin.
4. Look at where the pile ends up, not at the coin that was knocked out.
5. Try it again with a slow push instead of a flick, and compare.
ch8.u2.do.watch: A flick that is too high strikes two coins and the pile topples, which looks like a failed experiment and is actually a second force. Say so rather than letting them conclude the idea is wrong.
ask.ch8-u2-do-2.whyfast.q: Why does the hit have to be fast?
ask.ch8-u2-do-2.whyfast.a:
Because a slow push gives friction time to work.

The coins in the pile are pressed against each other, and friction between them can carry a sideways force upwards through the stack. Push the bottom coin gently and that friction has time to drag the ones above it along, and the whole pile travels together.

A fast strike is over before that can happen. The bottom coin is gone while the others are still standing still, which is the state the first law says they will stay in.
a.ch8-u2-do-2.title: Knock out the bottom coin
a.ch8-u2-do-2.blurb: A pile of carom coins and one sharp flick. Where does the pile end up?
ch8.u2.sort.i0.label: The bus pulls away from the stop while you are standing
ch8.u2.sort.i0.why: Your feet move off with the floor and the rest of you is still at rest, so you are left behind.
ch8.u2.sort.i1.label: The bus brakes hard at a junction
ch8.u2.sort.i1.why: You were moving with the bus and nothing has stopped you, so you keep going.
ch8.u2.sort.i2.label: The bus takes a sharp bend to the left
ch8.u2.sort.i2.why: You were travelling in a straight line and still are. It is the bus that has turned.
ch8.u2.sort.i3.label: The driver stamps on the accelerator on an open road
ch8.u2.sort.i3.why: Same as pulling away from the stop, only gentler and longer.
ch8.u2.sort.i4.label: The bus goes round a roundabout at a steady speed
ch8.u2.sort.i4.why: The speed is steady and the direction is not, and your body only cares about direction here.
ch8.u2.sort.i5.label: A seat belt is pulled tight across you in a crash
ch8.u2.sort.i5.why: The belt is there precisely because you would otherwise carry on into the seat in front.
a.ch8-u2-sort-3.title: Which way do you lurch?
a.ch8-u2-sort-3.blurb: Every one of these is the same law. Your body keeps doing what it was doing, and the bus does not.
ch8.u2.quiz.q0.prompt: An object has no net force on it at all. What can you say about it?
ch8.u2.quiz.q0.o0: It is at rest, or moving in a straight line at a steady speed
ch8.u2.quiz.q0.f0: Right. Both states are allowed, and the law treats them as the same case.
ch8.u2.quiz.q0.f1: Rest is one of the two possibilities, not the only one.
ch8.u2.quiz.q0.f2: Slowing down is a change of velocity, and that needs a force.
ch8.u2.quiz.q1.prompt: Why is luggage on the roof of a bus tied down with rope?
ch8.u2.quiz.q1.o0: Because it keeps moving when the bus stops, and would slide off the front
ch8.u2.quiz.q1.f0: Right. The bus is stopped by its brakes and the luggage is not, so it carries on.
ch8.u2.quiz.q1.o1: Because the wind would blow it away
ch8.u2.quiz.q1.f1: Wind matters a little. It is not why a rope is needed.
ch8.u2.quiz.q1.o2: Because it becomes heavier when the bus speeds up
ch8.u2.quiz.q1.f2: Mass does not change with speed at the speeds a bus manages.
ch8.u2.quiz.q2.prompt: Dust comes out of a carpet when it is beaten. Why?
ch8.u2.quiz.q2.o0: The carpet moves and the dust, at rest, stays behind
ch8.u2.quiz.q2.f0: Right. The dust has no force on it, so it keeps doing what it was doing, which is nothing.
ch8.u2.quiz.q2.o1: The stick knocks each speck of dust out individually
ch8.u2.quiz.q2.f1: A stick cannot find every speck. It only has to move the carpet.
ch8.u2.quiz.q2.o2: The beating heats the carpet and the dust rises
ch8.u2.quiz.q2.f2: No heating worth speaking of happens, and heat would not drive dust out anyway.
a.ch8-u2-quiz-4.title: The first law
ch8.u3.inertia:
Everything resists being started, and everything resists being stopped. That tendency has a name: inertia.

It is not a force and nothing supplies it. It is simply what the first law says, looked at from the object's side.

Objects differ in how much of it they have. An empty carton is easy to shove across a room and the same carton full of books is not. Kick a football and it flies; kick a stone of the same size and you hurt your foot. The thing that differs between them is mass, and that is the measurement: the mass of an object is the measure of its inertia. A train has more of it than a cart, which is why the same push does so much less to the train.

Its SI unit is the kilogram, and this is what a kilogram actually means.
a.ch8-u3-read-1.title: Inertia, and the number that measures it
ch8.u3.card.predict.prompt: A coin sits on a stiff card covering an empty glass. You flick the card sharply sideways. Where does the coin end up?
ch8.u3.card.predict.o0: It flies off sideways with the card
ch8.u3.card.predict.o1: It drops straight into the glass
ch8.u3.card.predict.o2: It stays balanced on the rim
ch8.u3.card.observe: Flick hard and flat. Then try pushing the card slowly and compare.
ch8.u3.card.explain:
The flick lasts a fraction of a second, so the card is gone before friction between the card and the coin has done anything much to the coin. The coin was at rest, nothing moved it sideways, and once its support vanished the only thing left acting on it was gravity.

Push the card slowly and the coin travels with it, because now friction has time to drag it along. The difference between the two attempts is not the force. It is the time the force had.
ch8.u3.do.steps:
1. Stand the empty tumbler on a table and lay the card flat over its mouth.
2. Put the coin in the middle of the card, right over the opening.
3. Flick the edge of the card hard and horizontally with one finger.
4. Note where the coin lands.
5. Reset, and this time slide the card away slowly. Note what the coin does now.
ch8.u3.do.watch: A flick that is angled upwards sends the coin with the card and looks like a failure of the idea. It is a second force, applied by the person. Have them keep the flick flat.
a.ch8-u3-do-2.title: Flick the card, keep the coin
a.ch8-u3-do-2.blurb: A coin on a card on a glass. Flick the card away and see where the coin goes.
ch8.u3.sort.i0.label: A loaded lorry
ch8.u3.sort.i0.why: More mass, so more of both: harder to get going and harder to pull up.
ch8.u3.sort.i1.label: A bicycle
ch8.u3.sort.i1.why: A few kilograms, and one leg is enough to start it.
ch8.u3.sort.i2.label: A stone the size of a football
ch8.u3.sort.i2.why: Same size as a football and many times the mass, which is why kicking it hurts.
ch8.u3.sort.i3.label: A five-rupee coin, next to a one-rupee coin
ch8.u3.sort.i3.why: The heavier coin needs the harder flick in Activity 8.2, and that is the whole measurement.
ch8.u3.sort.i4.label: A table tennis ball
ch8.u3.sort.i4.why: Almost no mass, which is why it can be stopped with a finger at speed.
ch8.u3.sort.i5.label: A goods train
ch8.u3.sort.i5.why: It needs more than a kilometre of track to stop, with the brakes full on.
ask.ch8-u3-sort-3.sizevsmass.q: A football and a stone are the same size. Why is the stone so much harder to kick?
ask.ch8-u3-sort-3.sizevsmass.a:
Because inertia follows mass, and mass is not size.

The stone has far more matter packed into the same volume. Kick both with the same force and the stone's acceleration is smaller by exactly the ratio of the masses, so it hardly moves while the football flies.

Your foot then takes the difference. The stone pushes back on you just as hard as you pushed on it, and because it did not move away, all of that push happened to your toes. That last part is the third law, and it is a few topics away.
a.ch8-u3-sort-3.title: Hard to start, hard to stop
a.ch8-u3-sort-3.blurb: More mass means more inertia, and more inertia shows up twice: in starting and in stopping.
ch8.u3.quiz.q0.prompt: What is the mass of an object a measure of?
ch8.u3.quiz.q0.f0: Right. More mass means more resistance to any change in its motion.
ch8.u3.quiz.q0.f1: An object does not have a force stored in it waiting to be used.
ch8.u3.quiz.q0.o2: How much space it takes up
ch8.u3.quiz.q0.f2: That is volume, and a stone and a football show how far the two can differ.
ch8.u3.quiz.q1.prompt: Which has more inertia: a rubber ball or a stone of the same size?
ch8.u3.quiz.q1.f0: Right, and you can feel the difference with one kick.
ch8.u3.quiz.q1.f1: Rubber is the lighter of the two, so it has less.
ch8.u3.quiz.q1.o2: They are the same, because the size is the same
ch8.u3.quiz.q1.f2: Size is not the measure. Mass is.
ch8.u3.quiz.q2.o0: No. It is the tendency of an object to resist a change in its motion
ch8.u3.quiz.q2.f0: Right. Nothing supplies it, and it has no direction and no newtons.
ch8.u3.quiz.q2.o1: Yes, and it pushes back when you shove something
ch8.u3.quiz.q2.f1: What pushes back is the third law's reaction, and that is a different idea with a different cause.
ch8.u3.quiz.q2.o2: Yes, and it is what keeps a moving object going
ch8.u3.quiz.q2.f2: Nothing is needed to keep a moving object going, which is exactly what the first law says.
a.ch8-u3-quiz-4.title: Inertia and mass
ch8.u4.momentum:
A truck parked on a roadside needs no attention from anyone. The same truck moving at 5 metres per second can kill a person standing in its path. A bullet has almost no mass at all and will do the same at a few hundred metres per second.

So neither quantity tells you much on its own. What matters is the two of them multiplied together, and Newton gave that product a name: momentum.

p = mv

It is measured in kilogram metres per second, kg m/s, and it carries a direction, the same direction as the velocity. A table tennis ball hit by a player does not hurt and a cricket ball at the same speed does, and the difference is entirely in the m.
a.ch8-u4-read-1.title: Mass and speed, taken together
ch8.u4.calc.c0.prompt: A cricket ball of mass 160 g is bowled at 25 m/s. What is its momentum?
ch8.u4.calc.c0.s0: The kilogram is the SI unit, so 160 g is 0.16 kg
ch8.u4.calc.c0.trap: Leaving the mass in grams and answering 4000. The unit of momentum has a kilogram in it.
ch8.u4.calc.c1.prompt: A lorry of mass 4000 kg is moving at 15 m/s. What is its momentum?
ch8.u4.calc.c1.trap: Nothing tricky here, which is the point: compare this with the cricket ball.
ch8.u4.calc.c2.prompt: A hockey ball of mass 200 g is travelling at 10 m/s. It is struck so that it comes straight back at 5 m/s. What is the size of the change in its momentum?
ch8.u4.calc.c2.s0: Momentum carries a direction, so call one way positive and the other negative
ch8.u4.calc.c2.s1: Before: 0.2 times 10, which is 2 kg m/s
ch8.u4.calc.c2.s2: After: 0.2 times minus 5, which is minus 1 kg m/s
ch8.u4.calc.c2.trap: Answering 1, by subtracting the speeds and ignoring that the ball turned round. A reversal makes the change bigger, not smaller.
ask.ch8-u4-calc-2.direction.q: Why does a ball coming back give a bigger change than a ball simply stopping?
ask.ch8-u4-calc-2.direction.a:
Because stopping removes the momentum it had, and turning round removes that and then supplies the same amount again the other way.

Take the hockey ball. Stopping it dead is a change of 2 kg m/s. Sending it back at 5 m/s is a change of 3 kg m/s, half as much again, from a stick travelling no faster.

This is why a wall you bounce off pushes harder than a wall you stick to, and why a cricketer takes a catch with soft hands rather than a hard flat palm.
a.ch8-u4-calc-2.title: Working out momentum
ch8.u4.quiz.q0.prompt: What is the momentum of an object of mass m moving with velocity v?
ch8.u4.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and its unit is kg m/s.
ch8.u4.quiz.q0.f1: That is the kinetic energy, which is chapter 10 and a different quantity.
ch8.u4.quiz.q0.f2: Squaring the velocity is not part of this one.
ch8.u4.quiz.q1.prompt: A parked lorry and a flying bullet. Which has the greater momentum?
ch8.u4.quiz.q1.o0: The bullet, because the lorry is not moving
ch8.u4.quiz.q1.f0: Right. A velocity of zero makes the whole product zero, whatever the mass is.
ch8.u4.quiz.q1.o1: The lorry, because it is far heavier
ch8.u4.quiz.q1.f1: Mass alone is not momentum. Multiply by the velocity and the lorry's comes to nothing.
ch8.u4.quiz.q1.f2: One of them is zero and the other is not.
ch8.u4.quiz.q2.o0: Yes, the same direction as the velocity
ch8.u4.quiz.q2.f0: Right, which is why a ball that turns round has had a bigger change than one that stops.
ch8.u4.quiz.q2.o1: No, it is just a number
ch8.u4.quiz.q2.f1: A quantity with mass times a direction in it has a direction.
ch8.u4.quiz.q2.o2: Yes, always along the direction of the force
ch8.u4.quiz.q2.f2: The force changes the momentum. It does not have to point the same way the momentum does.
a.ch8-u4-quiz-3.title: Momentum
ch8.u5.lab.predict.prompt: You push a trolley with a steady 6 newtons and note its acceleration. You then make the trolley twice as heavy and push with the same 6 newtons. What is the new acceleration?
ch8.u5.lab.observe: Run the second and third tasks one after the other and compare the slopes of the velocity-time lines.
ch8.u5.lab.explain:
Double the mass with the same force and the acceleration halves. Double the force at the same mass and the acceleration doubles. Both statements are the same equation seen from two sides.

a = F / m, which is usually written F = ma.

That is the second law, and it is also where the newton comes from: one newton is the force that gives one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared.
ch8.u5.lab.t1.label: 1 kg, pushed with 3 newtons.
ch8.u5.lab.t1.asks: Read the acceleration. Write it down before you change anything.
ch8.u5.lab.t2.label: 1 kg, pushed with 6 newtons.
ch8.u5.lab.t2.asks: Same trolley, twice the push. What happened to the acceleration, and to the slope of the velocity-time line?
ch8.u5.lab.t3.label: 2 kg, pushed with 6 newtons.
ch8.u5.lab.t3.asks: Twice the push and twice the mass, and the acceleration is back where it started. Write down the rule that covers both.
ch8.u5.lab.closing: F = ma. Double the force and the acceleration doubles. Double the mass and it halves. Nothing else in the chapter is needed to work out a force.
a.ch8-u5-lab-1.title: The same push on two different trolleys
a.ch8-u5-lab-1.blurb: Two sliders and one question: what does each of them do to the acceleration?
ch8.u5.catching:
The second law is usually met as F = ma. It began as something slightly different: a force is the rate at which momentum changes. Same statement, more useful shape.

Watch a fielder take a hard catch. The ball's momentum has to come down to zero either way, so the change in momentum is fixed before he touches it. What he controls is the time. Pull the hands back with the ball and that change is spread over a tenth of a second instead of a hundredth, and the force on his palms is a tenth of what it would have been.

The same idea is everywhere once you look. A high jumper lands on a thick mattress. A karate blow does the opposite, putting the whole change into the shortest time anyone can manage, and that is why it breaks the slab.

You cannot change how much momentum has to go. You can nearly always change how long it takes.
a.ch8-u5-read-2.title: Why a fielder pulls his hands back
ch8.u5.calc.c0.prompt: A steady force acts on a 5 kg object for 2 s and raises its velocity from 3 m/s to 7 m/s. Find the force.
ch8.u5.calc.c0.s0: First the acceleration: (7 minus 3) over 2, which is 2 m/s²
ch8.u5.calc.c0.trap: Multiplying the mass by the final velocity. Force comes from the change in velocity, not the velocity itself.
ch8.u5.calc.c1.prompt: Which needs the greater force: giving a 2 kg mass an acceleration of 5 m/s², or a 4 kg mass an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
ch8.u5.calc.c1.s0: Work out both with F = ma
ch8.u5.calc.c1.s3: Give the larger of the two
ch8.u5.calc.c1.trap: Picking the heavier mass on sight. The product decides it, and here the lighter one wins.
ch8.u5.calc.c2.prompt: A car of mass 1000 kg, with its passengers, is moving at 30 m/s. The brakes bring it to rest in 4 s. What force do the brakes apply?
ch8.u5.calc.c2.s0: a = (0 minus 30) over 4, which is minus 7.5 m/s²
ch8.u5.calc.c2.trap: Dropping the minus sign. It is saying the force points against the motion, which for a brake is the whole point.
ch8.u5.calc.c3.prompt: A force of 5 N gives a mass m1 an acceleration of 10 m/s², and a mass m2 an acceleration of 20 m/s². What acceleration would 5 N give if the two were tied together?
ch8.u5.calc.c3.s0: Find each mass from m = F/a: 5 over 10 is 0.5 kg, and 5 over 20 is 0.25 kg
ch8.u5.calc.c3.s1: Tied together they are one object of 0.75 kg
ch8.u5.calc.c3.trap: Averaging 10 and 20 to get 15. Masses add; accelerations do not.
ask.ch8-u5-calc-3.negative.q: What does a negative force actually mean?
ask.ch8-u5-calc-3.negative.a:
That it points the other way.

A force is a quantity with a direction, and once you have picked which way counts as positive, everything else has to follow that choice. Call the car's direction of travel positive and the brakes come out negative, because they are pushing backwards along it.

The size is 7500 N either way. The sign is not part of the size; it is the answer to a separate question, which is which way. Dropping it loses that answer, and in a problem with several forces it loses the arithmetic too.
a.ch8-u5-calc-3.title: Using F = ma
ch8.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: One newton is the force that gives:
ch8.u5.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and that is why the newton is also written kg m/s².
ch8.u5.quiz.q0.f1: A force does not give a velocity. It gives an acceleration.
ch8.u5.quiz.q0.f2: The kilogram is the SI unit here, not the gram.
ch8.u5.quiz.q1.prompt: The same force acts on a heavy trolley and a light one. What differs?
ch8.u5.quiz.q1.f0: Right. a = F/m, so a bigger m underneath means a smaller a.
ch8.u5.quiz.q1.f1: More mass means more resistance to being accelerated, not less.
ch8.u5.quiz.q1.o2: Both accelerate the same, because the force is the same
ch8.u5.quiz.q1.f2: That would be true only if the masses were equal.
ch8.u5.quiz.q2.prompt: A fielder pulls his hands back while taking a hard catch. Why?
ch8.u5.quiz.q2.o0: To stretch the stop over a longer time, which lowers the force
ch8.u5.quiz.q2.f0: Right. The change in momentum is fixed; the time it takes is not.
ch8.u5.quiz.q2.o1: To reduce the momentum the ball arrives with
ch8.u5.quiz.q2.f1: The ball's momentum when it arrives is already decided. Nothing he does changes it.
ch8.u5.quiz.q2.o2: To make the ball slow down before it reaches him
ch8.u5.quiz.q2.f2: Nothing he does to his hands affects the ball before it gets there.
a.ch8-u5-quiz-4.title: The second law
ch8.u6.lab.predict.prompt: Two carts sit on a smooth floor with a compressed spring between them. Cart A is four times as heavy as cart B. You let the spring go. Which cart ends up with the larger momentum?
ch8.u6.lab.predict.o0: Cart A, because it is heavier
ch8.u6.lab.predict.o1: Cart B, because it moves faster
ch8.u6.lab.predict.o2: Both the same size, in opposite directions
ch8.u6.lab.observe: Run the second task and watch the two momentum bars rather than the carts.
ch8.u6.lab.explain:
The spring pushes on both carts with the same force, for the same length of time, because it is one spring touching both of them. So each cart leaves with the same amount of momentum, and the bars come out the same length every time.

The speeds are a different matter. The light cart has to move four times as fast to carry the same momentum, and it does. Equal forces, equal momenta, very unequal speeds: that is the third law and the second law working together, and it is the thing a printed picture cannot show.
ch8.u6.lab.t1.label: Both carts 4 kg.
ch8.u6.lab.t1.asks: Equal masses. Compare the two speeds, and then the two momentum bars.
ch8.u6.lab.t2.label: Cart A 8 kg, cart B 2 kg.
ch8.u6.lab.t2.asks: One is four times the other. How many times faster does the light one go, and what did the bars do?
ch8.u6.lab.t3.label: Cart A 20 kg, cart B 0.2 kg.
ch8.u6.lab.t3.asks: A hundred to one. Cart A barely moves and cart B is gone. Are the forces on them still equal?
ch8.u6.lab.closing: The forces are always equal and the momenta are always equal. Only the speeds differ, and they differ because the masses do.
ask.ch8-u6-lab-1.gun.q: Is this what happens when a gun is fired?
ask.ch8-u6-lab-1.gun.a:
Yes, and it is the clearest everyday case of it.

The expanding gas pushes the bullet forwards and pushes the gun backwards, with the same force, for the same fraction of a second. The bullet and the gun therefore leave with the same amount of momentum in opposite directions.

The bullet is perhaps a thousandth of the mass of the gun, so it goes about a thousand times faster. That is the recoil you feel in your shoulder: not a smaller force than the one on the bullet, just the same force arriving at something much harder to move.

A sailor stepping off a boat gets the same deal, and so does anyone who has stood up too fast in a canoe.
a.ch8-u6-lab-1.title: One spring, two carts
a.ch8-u6-lab-1.blurb: A compressed spring between two carts. You set the masses; the spring pushes both with the same force for the same time.
ch8.u6.third:
The third law says that when one object pushes a second, the second pushes back on the first, at the same instant, equally hard and in the opposite direction. Forces always come in pairs. There is no such thing as one on its own.

Walking is the case worth holding on to. You accelerate forwards, so something must be pushing you forwards, and it is not your muscles: they only push your foot backwards against the road. The road pushes your foot forwards, and that is what moves you. On sheet ice, where the road cannot push back, nothing you do with your legs gets you anywhere.

Now the part that undoes most people. Push a parked truck and it pushes back on you just as hard. A student will say the two cancel and that is why it does not move.

They cannot cancel, because they are not on the same thing. Your push is on the truck; the truck's push is on you. Forces only cancel when they act on one object, and these two never do. The truck stays put because your push is small compared with the friction holding it, which is a completely separate sum, done on the truck alone.
a.ch8-u6-read-2.title: Why the parked truck does not move
ch8.u6.bag.predict.prompt: Two students stand on separate carts with wheels, facing each other and not moving. One throws a heavy bag of sand to the other. What happens?
ch8.u6.bag.predict.o3: Neither moves, because the bag is not touching the ground
ch8.u6.bag.observe: Mark the starting position of both carts with chalk and look at the two marks afterwards.
ch8.u6.bag.explain:
The thrower pushes the bag forwards, so the bag pushes the thrower backwards, and that cart rolls away. The bag then arrives at the catcher and pushes him backwards too as he stops it.

So both carts move, in opposite directions, from one throw. The lighter student moves further, because the same push has less mass to work on.
ch8.u6.do.steps:
1. Have two students stand on separate carts, a few metres apart and facing each other.
2. Chalk a line on the floor at each cart's wheels, so the starting positions are recorded.
3. One student throws the bag to the other. Both should keep their feet still.
4. Chalk the new positions and measure how far each cart travelled.
5. Throw it back and measure again.
6. Swap the students round, so the heavier one throws, and compare the distances.
ch8.u6.do.watch: Someone will push off with a foot without noticing, and that is a second force from the floor. Keep the feet on the cart, and have a third student watching for it.
a.ch8-u6-do-3.title: Throw a bag and move backwards
a.ch8-u6-do-3.blurb: Two students on wheeled boards, one heavy bag, and nothing else needed.
ch8.u6.sort.bin.1: Two forces on the same object
ch8.u6.sort.i0.label: Your foot pushes the road backwards, and the road pushes your foot forwards
ch8.u6.sort.i0.why: One force on the road and one on your foot. Two objects, so they can never cancel.
ch8.u6.sort.i1.label: A book's weight pulls it down, and the table pushes it up
ch8.u6.sort.i1.why: Both act on the book. They cancel, which is why it lies there, and that is balance rather than the third law.
ch8.u6.sort.i2.label: The gas pushes the bullet forwards, and the bullet pushes the gun backwards
ch8.u6.sort.i2.why: Different objects, same force, same instant.
ch8.u6.sort.i3.label: You push a crate, and friction from the floor resists the crate
ch8.u6.sort.i3.why: Both are on the crate. Whether it moves is decided by which is bigger.
ch8.u6.sort.i4.label: A swimmer pushes the water backwards, and the water pushes the swimmer forwards
ch8.u6.sort.i4.why: One on the water, one on the swimmer. This is the whole of swimming.
ch8.u6.sort.i5.label: The earth pulls the moon, and the moon pulls the earth
ch8.u6.sort.i5.why: Equal and opposite, on two different bodies, and the earth does move a little.
a.ch8-u6-sort-4.title: Is it really a pair?
a.ch8-u6-sort-4.blurb: An action-reaction pair acts on two different objects. Two forces on one object are something else entirely.
ch8.u6.quiz.q0.prompt: A student pushes a parked truck and it does not move. Do the action and reaction cancel each other?
ch8.u6.quiz.q0.o0: No. They act on different objects, so they can never cancel
ch8.u6.quiz.q0.f0: Right. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object, and these two never do.
ch8.u6.quiz.q0.o1: Yes, and that is exactly why the truck stays put
ch8.u6.quiz.q0.f1: They are on two different things. The truck stays put because friction on it beats the push on it.
ch8.u6.quiz.q0.o2: Yes, because the truck is heavier than the student
ch8.u6.quiz.q0.f2: Mass does not decide whether forces cancel. Which object they act on does.
ch8.u6.quiz.q1.prompt: A gun is fired. How does the force on the bullet compare with the force on the gun?
ch8.u6.quiz.q1.o0: They are equal in size and opposite in direction
ch8.u6.quiz.q1.f0: Right, and the accelerations are wildly different because the masses are.
ch8.u6.quiz.q1.o1: The force on the bullet is much larger
ch8.u6.quiz.q1.f1: The bullet accelerates much more, which is not the same statement.
ch8.u6.quiz.q1.o2: The force on the gun is much larger
ch8.u6.quiz.q1.f2: Nothing makes the gun's share bigger. It is simply harder to move.
ch8.u6.quiz.q2.prompt: What pushes you forwards when you walk?
ch8.u6.quiz.q2.o0: The road, pushing your foot forwards
ch8.u6.quiz.q2.f0: Right. You push the road backwards and it returns the favour, which is why ice defeats you.
ch8.u6.quiz.q2.o1: Your leg muscles, pushing you along
ch8.u6.quiz.q2.f1: Your muscles push your foot backwards against the road. The forward push comes from outside you.
ch8.u6.quiz.q2.f2: Something external has to push you, or your velocity could not change at all.
a.ch8-u6-quiz-5.title: The third law
mis.motion-needs-a-force.statement: A moving object needs a force to keep it moving.
mis.motion-needs-a-force.correction: It needs one only to change how it is moving. Remove everything and it carries straight on, which is the first law.
mis.unbalanced-holds-things-still.statem: An unbalanced force holds an object where it is.
mis.unbalanced-holds-things-still.correc: It is the one thing that cannot. An unbalanced force always changes the velocity.
mis.steady-speed-needs-a-net-force.state: An object moving at a steady speed has a net force pushing it along.
mis.steady-speed-needs-a-net-force.corre: A steady velocity means nothing is left over. The push and the resistance have come into balance.
mis.steady-speed-means-no-forces.stateme: An object moving at a steady speed has no forces on it.
mis.steady-speed-means-no-forces.correct: It can have several, all cancelling. Nothing left over is not the same as nothing there.
mis.no-motion-no-friction.statement: If nothing is moving, there is no friction.
mis.no-motion-no-friction.correction: Friction is at its busiest then. The floor supplies exactly as much as the push, right up to its limit.
mis.friction-can-drive.statement: Friction can set a stationary object moving.
mis.friction-can-drive.correction: It only ever opposes. It can slow a thing down or hold it still, and never start it off.
mis.friction-points-down.statement: Friction pushes down into the surface.
mis.friction-points-down.correction: That is the object's weight. Friction acts along the surface, against the way the object is going.
mis.circular-motion-is-balanced.statemen: A ball swung on a string at a steady speed has balanced forces on it.
mis.circular-motion-is-balanced.correcti: Its direction changes at every instant, which is a change of velocity, and that takes an unbalanced force.
mis.no-force-means-at-rest.statement: An object with no net force on it must be at rest.
mis.no-force-means-at-rest.correction: It may also be moving in a straight line at a steady speed. The law treats the two as one case.
mis.no-force-means-slowing.statement: An object with no net force on it gradually slows down.
mis.no-force-means-slowing.correction: Slowing is a change of velocity and needs a force. What slows real objects is friction, not the absence of a push.
mis.rope-is-for-wind.statement: Roof luggage is roped down because of the wind.
mis.rope-is-for-wind.correction: It is roped because the bus can be stopped by its brakes and the luggage cannot.
mis.mass-changes-with-speed.statement: An object gets heavier as it speeds up.
mis.mass-changes-with-speed.correction: Not at any speed a bus manages. Mass is the same whether the object is parked or flying.
mis.stick-hits-the-dust.statement: Beating a carpet works because the stick strikes each speck of dust.
mis.stick-hits-the-dust.correction: The stick moves the carpet. The dust, with nothing acting on it, stays behind.
mis.beating-heats-the-carpet.statement: Beating a carpet warms it, and the dust rises with the heat.
mis.beating-heats-the-carpet.correction: Nothing is warmed worth speaking of, and heat would not drive dust sideways out of a carpet anyway.
mis.mass-is-stored-force.statement: An object's mass is a store of force it can apply.
mis.mass-is-stored-force.correction: Nothing stores force. Mass measures how hard the object is to accelerate.
mis.mass-is-size.statement: The bigger an object looks, the more inertia it has.
mis.mass-is-size.correction: A football and a stone of the same size settle that. Inertia follows mass, and mass is not volume.
mis.rubber-has-more-inertia.statement: A rubber ball has more inertia than a stone of the same size.
mis.rubber-has-more-inertia.correction: The stone has far more mass in the same space, and one kick tells you which is which.
mis.inertia-is-a-force.statement: Inertia is a force that pushes back when you shove something.
mis.inertia-is-a-force.correction: Nothing supplies it and it has no newtons. It is a name for the tendency the first law describes.
mis.momentum-is-half-mv-squared.statemen: Momentum is half the mass times the velocity squared.
mis.momentum-is-half-mv-squared.correcti: That is kinetic energy, which is chapter 10. Momentum is simply mass times velocity.
mis.momentum-squares-the-velocity.statem: Momentum is the mass times the velocity squared.
mis.momentum-squares-the-velocity.correc: There is no square in it. p = mv, and its unit is kg m/s.
mis.heavier-always-means-more-momentum.s: The heavier object always has the greater momentum.
mis.heavier-always-means-more-momentum.c: Not if it is standing still. A velocity of zero makes the whole product zero.
mis.parked-object-has-momentum.statement: An object standing still has some momentum, because it has mass.
mis.parked-object-has-momentum.correctio: Momentum is mass times velocity. A velocity of zero makes the whole product zero, however heavy the object is.
mis.momentum-has-no-direction.statement: Momentum is just a number, with no direction.
mis.momentum-has-no-direction.correction: It points the way the velocity points, which is why a ball that turns round has had a bigger change than one that stops.
mis.momentum-follows-the-force.statement: Momentum always points the way the force points.
mis.momentum-follows-the-force.correctio: The force changes the momentum. A braking car has momentum forwards and a force backwards.
mis.force-gives-velocity.statement: A force gives an object a velocity.
mis.force-gives-velocity.correction: It gives an acceleration. What velocity that works out to depends on how long the force acted.
mis.newton-uses-grams.statement: One newton accelerates one gram by one metre per second squared.
mis.newton-uses-grams.correction: One kilogram. The newton is defined in SI units, and the gram is not one.
mis.heavier-accelerates-more.statement: Under the same force, the heavier object accelerates more.
mis.heavier-accelerates-more.correction: a = F/m, so a larger mass underneath gives a smaller acceleration.
mis.same-force-same-acceleration.stateme: The same force always produces the same acceleration.
mis.same-force-same-acceleration.correct: Only on the same mass. That is the whole content of F = ma.
mis.catching-reduces-momentum.statement: Pulling the hands back reduces the momentum the ball arrives with.
mis.catching-reduces-momentum.correction: The ball's momentum on arrival is already fixed. What the fielder changes is how long the stop takes.
mis.catching-slows-the-ball-early.statem: Pulling the hands back makes the ball slow down before it is caught.
mis.catching-slows-the-ball-early.correc: Nothing he does with his hands reaches the ball before it gets there.
mis.action-and-reaction-cancel.statement: Action and reaction cancel each other, so nothing can ever move.
mis.action-and-reaction-cancel.correctio: They act on two different objects. Forces cancel only when they act on the same one.
mis.heavier-object-wins-the-pair.stateme: In an action-reaction pair the heavier object exerts the larger force.
mis.heavier-object-wins-the-pair.correct: The two forces are equal whatever the masses. Only the accelerations differ.
mis.bigger-acceleration-means-bigger-for: The object that accelerates more must have had the larger force on it.
Not when the masses differ. A bullet and a gun take the same force and the bullet has a thousandth of the mass.
mis.muscles-push-you-forward.statement: Your leg muscles push you forward when you walk.
mis.muscles-push-you-forward.correction: They push your foot backwards against the road. The forward push is the road's, which is why ice defeats you.
mis.you-push-yourself.statement: A person can push themselves forward without anything else being involved.
mis.you-push-yourself.correction: A change of velocity needs an external force. Without something to push against there is nowhere for it to come from.
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: A crate is sliding across a floor at a steady speed. Describe the forces acting along the floor on it.
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: Two of them, equal in size and opposite in direction: the push driving it and the friction resisting it. Nothing is left over, which is why the speed does not change.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'there is no force on it'. There are two, both hard at work. Nothing left over is not the same as nothing there.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: What is the one thing only an unbalanced force can do?
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: Change the velocity: make it bigger, make it smaller, or turn it in a new direction.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'it makes things move'. True but narrow. Slowing a moving thing and turning a corner both count, and neither is making anything move.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: Galileo imagined the second slope made completely flat. Tell me what he concluded.
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: That the marble would keep rolling forever, still looking for the height it started from. No force is needed to keep something moving.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'the marble would stop'. It does stop in any real experiment, and the whole argument is that friction is the reason rather than the nature of motion.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: You are standing in a bus that brakes hard. Which way do you go, and why?
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: Forwards. You were moving with the bus, the brakes stopped the bus, and nothing stopped you.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'the bus pushes me forwards'. Nothing pushed you at all. That is what makes it a first law question.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: What is the mass of an object a measure of?
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: Its inertia: how strongly it resists any change in its state of rest or of motion. The SI unit is the kilogram.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'how much space it takes up'. A football and a stone of the same size settle that one.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: Explain why the coin drops into the glass when the card is flicked away.
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: The flick is over before friction can drag the coin sideways, so the coin stays where it was. Its support then disappears and gravity takes it straight down.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'the card pushed it down'. The card went sideways, not down. What took the coin down was gravity, once there was nothing holding it up.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: Give the formula for momentum, and its unit.
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: p = mv, measured in kilogram metres per second, kg m/s, and pointing the same way as the velocity.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: Listen for the unit left off, or given as newtons. Momentum is not a force, and the mistake usually means the two have been merged.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: A hockey ball is struck so that it comes straight back. Why is the change in momentum larger than if it had simply stopped?
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: Because stopping it only removes the momentum it had. Turning it round removes that and then supplies the same thing again the other way, so the change is the two added together.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: Listen for the direction being dropped and the two speeds subtracted. The sign is what makes a reversal expensive.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: The same force acts on a 2 kg trolley and on a 6 kg trolley. Tell me what differs and what does not.
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: The force is the same on both, by assumption. The acceleration is not: a = F/m, so the 6 kg trolley accelerates a third as much.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'the heavier one accelerates more'. More mass means more resistance to being accelerated, which is the opposite.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: Explain why a high jumper lands on a thick mattress rather than on bare ground.
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: Her momentum has to come down to zero either way. The mattress stretches that change over a much longer time, and a slower change needs a smaller force.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because it is soft'. True, and the reason softness helps is the part worth having: it buys time, and the force falls in step with it.
recap.s.u6.q1.ask: A student pushes a parked truck and it will not move. Explain why the action and reaction do not cancel.
recap.s.u6.q1.answer: Because they act on two different objects. The student's push is on the truck and the truck's push is on the student, and forces can only cancel when they act on the same thing. The truck stays put because the friction on it is larger than the push on it, which is a separate sum done on the truck alone.
recap.s.u6.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'they do cancel, and that is why it does not move'. It is the commonest answer in the chapter and the exercise is written to catch exactly it.
recap.s.u6.q2.ask: Name the force that pushes you forwards when you walk, and say where it comes from.
recap.s.u6.q2.answer: The road's push on your foot. You push the road backwards and it pushes you forwards by the same amount.
recap.s.u6.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'my legs'. The legs push the foot backwards against the road. The forward push is the road's, which is why ice defeats the strongest legs.
aid.s.u6.meaning: Five questions that tell a balanced pair of forces from an action-reaction pair. The word is the hook: these are the basic checks, and the first one settles nearly every case on its own.
aid.s.u6.B.property: Bodies: how many objects are the two forces acting on?
aid.s.u6.B.a: One. Both are on the same object, which is exactly why they can cancel.
aid.s.u6.B.b: Two. One on each, every time, and never both on the same one.
aid.s.u6.A.a: Only when they happen to be. Unbalance them and the object accelerates.
aid.s.u6.A.b: Always, without exception, whatever the two objects are made of or weigh.
aid.s.u6.S.property: Simultaneous: do they appear and disappear together?
aid.s.u6.S.a: Not necessarily. Take one away and the other can carry on by itself.
aid.s.u6.S.b: Always. Neither of them exists for an instant without the other.
aid.s.u6.I.property: Interaction: do they come from one event?
aid.s.u6.I.a: Not necessarily. The two can have completely unrelated causes.
aid.s.u6.I.b: Always one interaction, looked at from each side in turn.
aid.s.u6.C.property: Cancel: can the two add up to nothing?
aid.s.u6.C.a: Yes, and that is what the word balanced means.
aid.s.u6.C.b: Never. They are on different objects, so there is nothing to add them up on.
gloss.force: A push, a pull or a hit. Nobody sees one; you see what it did, which is a change of speed, of direction or of shape.
gloss.balanced-forces: Two or more forces on one object that add up to nothing. The object's velocity does not change, whether it was moving or not.
gloss.unbalanced-forces: What is left over when the forces on an object have not cancelled. It is the only thing that can change a velocity.
gloss.net-force: The single force that would have the same effect as all the forces on an object put together. Zero when they are balanced.
gloss.friction: The force between two surfaces in contact that resists sliding. It always opposes motion and can never start any.
gloss.inertia: The tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion. Not a force, and nothing supplies it.
gloss.mass: The measure of an object's inertia, in kilograms. More mass means more resistance to being started or stopped.
gloss.first-law: An object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at a steady speed, unless an unbalanced force acts on it.
gloss.first-law.forms: first law of motion|first law|law of inertia
gloss.momentum: Mass times velocity, p = mv, in kg m/s. It carries the direction of the velocity, and it is what a force actually changes.
gloss.second-law: The rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied unbalanced force and points the same way. In practice, F = ma.
gloss.newton: The SI unit of force. One newton gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared, so it is also kg m/s squared.
gloss.acceleration: The change in velocity per unit time, in metres per second squared. It is what an unbalanced force produces.
gloss.third-law: When one object exerts a force on a second, the second exerts an equal and opposite force on the first, at the same instant.
gloss.action-reaction: The two forces of a third law pair. They are always equal, always opposite, and always on two different objects, which is why they never cancel.
